summary_html: Court issues a **protective or restraining order** to prevent contact, remove abuser, or ensure safety without removing the child. Federal law leaves implementation to states but funds protection efforts through CAPTA and IV-B.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — authorizes protective interventions and state plan requirements  
- **SSA Title IV-B** — permits funding for protective services and court interventions

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Meek
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the portion of an order continuing DSS custody based on the mother's conduct, holding she was entitled to notice that DSS would seek custody at the father's merits hearing, while holding that omission of the statutory boldface notices from the removal petition did not divest the family court of subject matter jurisdiction.
key_cases.relevance: Any order restricting a parent's custody or contact must be preceded by notice that the issue will be decided.
key_cases.quote: Mother's fundamental right to due process entitled her to notice that DSS intended to petition the family court for custody of the children at Father's hearing.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Wilson
key_cases.holding: The court held that a parent facing an intervention petition and entry on the Central Registry has a protected liberty interest and a due process right of confrontation, and that allowing the child to testify outside his presence without an individualized finding of trauma violated that right.
key_cases.relevance: Because intervention orders can restrict contact and compel counseling without removing the child, Wilson supplies the due process standard for those protective measures.
key_cases.quote: Because Wilson did not have the opportunity to be heard in a meaningful manner, his due process right was violated.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Headden
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed as modified the termination of the mother's parental rights, holding clear and convincing evidence established willful failure to visit and willful failure to support and that termination was in the child's best interest, and declining to reach the remaining statutory ground.
key_cases.relevance: The mother's visitation was terminated by a permanency planning order because she had not completed her treatment plan, making Headden the South Carolina illustration of contact being restricted as a protective measure short of removal or termination.
key_cases.quote: Grounds for termination of parental rights must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.

key_cases.case_name: Richland County Department of Social Services v. Earles
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that unavailability based on severe emotional trauma requires a finding that the child would be traumatized by testifying in person, by videotaped deposition and by closed-circuit television, that the record here supported that finding, and that clear and convincing evidence showed the home could not be made safe.
key_cases.relevance: Visitation had been ordered to cease because contact was traumatizing the children, and Earles is the South Carolina decision that measures that kind of protective restriction against evidence of severe emotional trauma.
key_cases.quote: Unavailability under § 19-1-180(B)(2)(a)(v) requires a finding that the child will suffer severe trauma by testifying under all three methods.
